specPoints.text: understand the differences between sexual and asexual reproduction

primer.text: One parent or two; clones or fresh shuffles; speed or resilience. Reproduction's biggest fork is sexual versus asexual, and this note walks both roads: gamete fusion and meiosis on one side, single-parent mitotic copying on the other, finishing with the comparison table examiners quote.

lessons.title: Sexual Reproduction
lessons.opening: Sexual reproduction fuses a male and a female gamete: two parents contribute genetic material, meiosis halves the chromosome count to build those gametes, and the resulting zygote divides by mitosis into an embryo that differs genetically from both parents.
keyPoints: Sexual reproduction builds offspring from the fusion of a male and a female gamete.
Offspring inherit genetic material from both parents and are genetically different from either.
Gametes are made by meiosis, a division that halves the chromosome number.
The fertilised zygote divides by mitosis and develops into an embryo.
Sexual reproduction therefore feeds fresh variation into a population, generation after generation.

low.restatement: Two parents, two half-cells, one shuffled whole cell — and every offspring a new combination.
low.analogy: Two playlists shuffled into one completely new mix.
low.examPointer: Keep the divisions straight: meiosis for gametes, mitosis after fertilisation.

medium.restatement: The shuffling happens twice: meiosis recombines genes inside each parent's gametes, and fertilisation pairs gametes from two different individuals, so each offspring carries a combination no parent held.
medium.analogy: A card game where both players deal new hands before the tables are even joined.
medium.examPointer: Say why variation matters — it feeds the population's response to change.

check.stem: What produces the offspring in sexual reproduction?

options.text: The fusion of male and female gametes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: The copying of one parent cell
options.explanation: Copying one parent is asexual reproduction.

options.text: The division of a single body cell
options.explanation: Body-cell division builds the body, not new offspring.
One zygote forms per fertilisation; zygotes do not merge.

check.stem: Which cell division makes gametes?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Mitosis copies cells identically for growth.
Fusion joins gametes; it does not make them.
Specialisation assigns cell jobs after division.

check.stem: How do sexually produced offspring compare with their parents?

options.text: They are genetically different from either parent
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: They are identical to the mother
options.explanation: Identical offspring happen in asexual reproduction.

options.text: They carry only the father's genes
options.explanation: Both parents contribute half.

options.text: They are exact clones of both parents
options.explanation: Cloning never happens in sexual reproduction.

check.stem: What does the zygote divide by as it becomes an embryo?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Meiosis made the gametes; the embryo grows by mitosis.
Fusion happened once, at fertilisation.
Mutation is random error, not a division type.

check.stem: Why does sexual reproduction introduce variation into populations?

options.text: Offspring combine genetic material from two parents in fresh ways
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Perfect copying preserves, it does not vary.

options.text: Because one parent alone decides traits
options.explanation: Two parents contribute.
Gametes carry recombined, unique sets.

check.stem: State the event that defines sexual reproduction.
check.modelAnswer: Sexual reproduction means offspring arise from the fusion of a male and a female gamete.

check.stem: Name the two types of cell division involved in sexual reproduction and their roles.
check.modelAnswer: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to produce gametes, and mitosis divides the zygote as it develops into an embryo.

check.stem: Explain why offspring of sexual reproduction are genetically unique.
check.modelAnswer: Each offspring inherits genetic material from both parents, and meiosis plus fertilisation recombine it, so no offspring matches either parent's genome.

check.stem: A population faces a new disease. Explain why its sexually produced members give the species an edge.
check.modelAnswer: Sexual reproduction has introduced variation, so some individuals carry gene combinations that resist the disease and can survive to reproduce.

lessons.title: Asexual Reproduction
lessons.opening: Asexual reproduction needs one parent only: no gametes, no fertilisation, no mixing. Mitosis copies the genome, the offspring are clones of the parent and each other, and the speed gained trades away the variation that guards a population against disease and change.
keyPoints: Asexual reproduction produces offspring from a single parent.
No gametes or fertilisation are involved, and no genetic information is mixed.
Every offspring is a genetic copy of the parent and of every sibling clone.
The process is quicker and more efficient than sexual reproduction.
Lack of variation leaves populations vulnerable to disease or environmental change.

low.restatement: One parent copies itself; every offspring is the same, and fast.
low.analogy: A photocopier running overnight: hundreds of identical pages by morning.
low.examPointer: Pair the advantage (speed) with the cost (no variation) — the trade-off is the point.

medium.restatement: The efficiency is real: no mate-finding, no gamete waste, every cell able to reproduce. The bill comes later, because a pathogen that defeats one clone defeats them all, and no genetic reshuffle stands ready for a changed environment.
medium.analogy: One password for every account: convenient until a single breach unlocks everything.
medium.examPointer: Use the words clones and genetically identical — they are the mark-scheme anchors.

check.stem: How many parents does asexual reproduction require?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Two parents is the sexual count.

options.text: One per generation only in plants
options.explanation: Asexual reproduction in animals also uses one parent.
A parent supplies the genetic copy.

check.stem: Which processes are absent from asexual reproduction?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Mitosis drives the cloning itself.
Those are its core features.
Offspring obviously exist.

check.stem: How do asexually produced offspring compare genetically?

options.text: They clone the parent exactly and match one another as well
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Clones match one another.

options.text: They carry half of each parent's genes
options.explanation: There is only one parent and no halving.
Uniqueness belongs to sexual reproduction.

check.stem: What advantage does asexual reproduction offer over sexual reproduction?

options.text: It happens more quickly and efficiently
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Its offspring lack variation.

options.text: It halves the chromosome number freshly each time
options.explanation: No meiosis runs in asexual reproduction.

options.text: It mixes genes from two lines
options.explanation: No mixing occurs.

check.stem: A fungal disease sweeps a field of cloned plants. Why does the whole crop risk loss?

options.text: With no genetic variation, what infects one clone can infect them all
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Mutation is random, not a guaranteed rescue.
Identical genomes give identical responses.

options.text: Sexual reproduction runs inside the crop
options.explanation: The crop is clonal; no gamete mixing occurs.

check.stem: State what asexual reproduction produces from a single parent.
check.modelAnswer: Asexual reproduction produces offspring that are genetically identical clones of the single parent.

check.stem: State the cost of asexual reproduction's lack of variation.
check.modelAnswer: With nothing to vary, a population faces disease or environmental change far more exposed.

check.stem: Explain why no fertilisation occurs in asexual reproduction.
check.modelAnswer: One parent cell alone is enough, so no second gamete arrives and nothing mixes.

check.stem: A greenhouse grower relies on cloned cuttings. State one benefit and one risk of that choice.
check.modelAnswer: The benefit is fast, efficient production of identical plants, and the risk is that a single disease could sweep every clone since none vary genetically.

lessons.title: Comparing the Two Modes
lessons.opening: The two modes line up on three axes: parent count (one versus two), the divisions used (mitosis alone versus meiosis then mitosis) and the offspring's genetics (identical clones versus unique individuals).
keyPoints: Asexual reproduction uses one parent; sexual reproduction uses two.
Asexual offspring are made by mitosis; sexual reproduction uses meiosis to make gametes and mitosis after fertilisation.
Asexual offspring are genetically identical to each other and the parent.
Sexual offspring are genetically unique and different from both parents.

low.restatement: One versus two parents, mitosis versus meiosis-plus-mitosis, clones versus unique offspring.
low.analogy: Photocopying a book versus co-writing a new one with a co-author.
low.examPointer: Reproduce the three-row comparison — parents, divisions, genetics.

medium.restatement: Every contrast traces back to one design choice: whether genetic information is copied or recombined, and each mode's division machinery, parent count and offspring genetics follow from that choice.
medium.analogy: Two publishing models: a reprint of a bestseller versus a fresh collaboration.
medium.examPointer: In table answers, keep the columns aligned to the mode — mixing them loses marks.

check.stem: Which comparison row contrasts mitosis alone with meiosis followed by mitosis?

options.text: The row about the cell divisions that build the offspring
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That row contrasts one parent with two.
That row contrasts clones with unique offspring.
Speed is not one of the three table rows.

check.stem: Which mode produces genetically unique offspring, and why?

options.text: Sexual reproduction, because genetic material from two parents recombines
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Asexual reproduction, because mitosis varies genes
options.explanation: Mitosis copies genes without variation.

options.text: Asexual reproduction, because two parents mix
options.explanation: Asexual uses one parent.
Mutation is not the taught source of uniqueness.

check.stem: How many parent cells does asexual reproduction use, compared with sexual reproduction?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The order is reversed.
Sexual reproduction needs two parents.
Only sexual reproduction uses two.

check.stem: A biology exam asks for the genetic similarity of asexual offspring. What is the correct cell?

options.text: Identical clones of one another and of the parent
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Uniqueness belongs in the sexual column.
Clones match the parent.
Asexual reproduction gives no mixture.

check.stem: Which statement correctly completes the comparison table for sexual reproduction?

options.text: Meiosis produces the gametes, then mitosis follows fertilisation
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The zygote grows by mitosis.
Gametes come from meiosis.
Both divisions appear in sequence.

check.stem: State the number of parent cells in each reproduction mode.
check.modelAnswer: Asexual reproduction uses one parent cell and sexual reproduction uses two.

check.stem: State the genetic similarity of offspring in each mode.
check.modelAnswer: Asexual offspring are genetically identical clones, while sexual offspring are genetically unique and different from both parents.

check.stem: Explain why the division row of the comparison table mentions both meiosis and mitosis for sexual reproduction.
check.modelAnswer: Meiosis first produces the haploid gametes, and after fertilisation mitosis divides the zygote as it grows into an embryo, so both divisions appear in the sexual column.

check.stem: Complete a three-row comparison for bacteria dividing by copying versus flowering plants pairing by gametes.
check.modelAnswer: The bacterial route matches asexual reproduction with one parent, mitotic copying and identical offspring, while the plant route matches sexual reproduction with two parents, meiosis then mitosis and unique offspring.

glossary.definition: Reproduction by fusion of male and female gametes, producing genetically different offspring.
Reproduction from a single parent producing genetically identical clones.
The cell division that halves the chromosome number to make gametes.
The cell division that copies cells identically, used in growth and asexual reproduction.
